sections.heading: Receiving a gospel I could never have invented
sections.text: Lord Jesus, no one could have dreamed up this good news. It did not come from human imagination or religious effort. In eternal grace, you came not only to announce the gospel but to be the gospel for me. You lived among us with compassion that never ran dry. You took insult, cruelty, and death into yourself so that I could be bought back, rescued, and set free.
theological_themes: The gospel is God’s revelation, not a human invention.
Jesus Christ is both the messenger of salvation and the substance of salvation.
Christ’s suffering and death redeem and liberate sinners.

scripture_references.connection: Paul insists that the gospel he preached was not a human construction but came through revelation from Jesus Christ. This supports the prayer’s wonder that the gospel could not have been conceived or invented by human wisdom.

Jesus describes his own mission as serving and giving his life as a ransom for many. That directly grounds the prayer’s language of being redeemed, ransomed, and freed through Christ’s costly self-giving.

sections.heading: Praising the Father, Son, and Spirit for salvation
sections.text: Father, thank you for planning this way of mercy before I ever knew I needed it. Lamb of God, thank you for opening the way through your own blood. Holy Spirit, thank you for bringing this gospel home to my heart, making it more than words I hear from the outside. Triune God, press the gospel deep into me until it touches every part of who I am—what I think, what I love, what I choose, what I say, and how I live.
theological_themes: Salvation is the work of the triune God: planned by the Father, accomplished by the Son, and applied by the Spirit.
The gospel must be inwardly received and personally worked into the whole life.
True faith involves hearing, confessing, feeling, and living the truth of Christ.

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents salvation in a distinctly Trinitarian shape: the Father chooses and purposes, the Son redeems through his blood, and the Spirit seals believers. It fits the prayer’s praise of Father, Son, and Spirit for one united work of grace.

Paul teaches that believers receive the Spirit so they may understand what God has freely given. This supports the prayer’s request that the Spirit apply the gospel to the heart rather than leaving it as external information.

sections.heading: Letting the gospel rule my whole life
sections.text: Teach me not to treat this blessing lightly. Help me turn away from every sin I still protect and excuse. Bring my heart and my daily life under the authority of your good news. Let the gospel shape my desires, govern my choices, correct my thinking, and reorder my loves. Make me steady and honest in following you—not bending your truth for comfort, advantage, reputation, safety, or convenience.
theological_themes: The gospel calls for repentance from cherished sin.
Grace trains believers into obedience rather than leaving them unchanged.
Christian faithfulness must not be compromised for personal gain or self-protection.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the grace of God not only brings salvation but trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, godly lives. This anchors the prayer’s plea for the gospel to rule desires, conduct, and habits.

Jesus calls his disciples to deny themselves and follow him, even when self-preservation and worldly gain pull the other way. This supports the prayer’s refusal to depart from Christ for advantage or to avoid difficulty.

sections.heading: Coming back to the cross with nothing to boast in
sections.text: Take me again to the cross. Teach me to see your glory in what the world calls shame. Strip away every comfortable claim that I am acceptable because of what I have done, how I have performed, or how I compare with other people. Leave me with Christ alone—his wounds, his obedience, his mercy, his righteousness—as my only confidence before you.
theological_themes: The cross overturns worldly ideas of glory and shame.
Self-righteousness must be renounced before God.
The believer’s confidence is Christ’s righteousness, not personal achievement.

scripture_references.connection: Paul refuses to boast in anything except the cross of Christ, even though crucifixion was a sign of public disgrace. This illuminates the prayer’s request to find glory in the cross’s apparent shame.

Paul counts his former religious credentials as loss so that he may be found in Christ with a righteousness from God through faith. This directly supports the prayer’s renunciation of righteousness based on personal doing.

sections.heading: Confessing how long I have resisted you
sections.text: Gracious Redeemer, I have pushed you aside for too long. I have treated your mercy as small, delayed repentance, and lived as if your wounds did not matter. My sin has dishonored you, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Thank you for the patience that has carried me all this time. Thank you for the grace that now makes me willing to belong to you.
theological_themes: Sin is not merely failure but personal offense against Christ.
God’s patience toward sinners is mercy, not indifference.
Willing repentance is itself a gift of grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul presents himself as a sinner who received mercy so that Christ’s perfect patience might be displayed. This supports the prayer’s gratitude that Christ has borne patiently with prolonged neglect and sin.

Paul teaches that God’s kindness and patience are meant to lead sinners to repentance. This fits the prayer’s movement from confessing impenitence to thanking God for grace that makes the heart willing.

sections.heading: Asking to be held close to Christ forever
sections.text: Lord Jesus, join me to yourself with bonds I cannot break. Hold me so closely that no temptation, fear, pride, suffering, success, or hidden sin can pull me away from you. Keep me yours—because you are my Lord, my Savior, and my only hope.
theological_themes: Believers need Christ to preserve them, not merely to begin their faith.
Union with Christ is the ground of lasting security and fruitfulness.
The Christian’s final hope is belonging to Jesus.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that disciples must abide in him because apart from him they can do nothing. This grounds the prayer’s request to be united to Christ in a living, dependent bond.
Paul declares that nothing in creation can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus. This supports the prayer’s longing that nothing would ever draw the believer back from Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about having 'often crucified thee' and 'crucified thee afresh' echoes severe New Testament language about apostasy and public contempt for Christ. In this adaptation it is rendered as dishonoring Christ through impenitence and treating his wounds lightly, rather than implying Christ is literally re-crucified or that the praying believer is beyond repentance.

The original’s strong demand for strict adherence without departing 'in any instance' could be misunderstood as perfectionism or legalism. It has been preserved as a prayer for uncompromising faithfulness grounded in the gospel, not as a claim that obedience earns acceptance with God.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Messenger and message' was rendered as Christ both announcing and embodying the gospel, because the original holds together Jesus’ proclamation, person, life, suffering, and saving work.
'Secure this mighty blessing' was interpreted not as earning salvation but as taking hold of the gospel seriously through repentance, faith, and obedient surrender.
'Every darling lust' was expressed as sins I still protect and excuse, preserving the concrete force of cherished sin while using contemporary language.

The closing request for 'inseparable bonds' was expressed in terms of union with Christ and his preserving grace, keeping the prayer’s dependence on Christ rather than turning it into self-generated resolve.
